Azekah
uh-ZEE-kuh
proper noun
Hebrew Azeqah, perhaps “tilled” or “dug over,” a fortified town in the lowland of Judah.

📖 Biblical Definition

Azekah was a fenced city in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah, set on the road that descended from the hill country toward the Philistine plain. It was unto Azekah that the LORD chased the five Amorite kings in the great battle for Gibeon, casting down upon them the great hailstones from heaven, so that more died of the hail than of the sword (Josh 10:11). The town was reckoned among the cities of Judah’s lowland (Josh 15:35) and was fortified by Rehoboam among the defences of the kingdom (2Ch 11:9). It was between Shochoh and Azekah, at Ephes-dammim, that the Philistines pitched their camp when Goliath defied the armies of the living God and David slew him with a sling and a stone (1Sa 17:1). In the last days of Judah, when Nebuchadnezzar’s army was sweeping the land, Azekah and Lachish were the only fenced cities that remained, and the prophet Jeremiah names them as the last to fall (Jer 34:7). Azekah thus stands at the beginning and the ending of Judah’s story in the land: a witness to the LORD’s deliverance by hailstones and by a shepherd’s sling, and a witness to the judgment that at last overtook a people who would not return to their God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A fortified town in the lowland of Judah, near the field of David and Goliath; one of the last cities to fall to Babylon.

expand to see more

AZEKAH, a fenced city in the Shephelah, the lowland of Judah.

Unto it the LORD chased the Amorite kings with hailstones from heaven (Josh 10:11).

It was reckoned among the lowland cities of Judah (Josh 15:35).

The Philistines pitched near it before David slew Goliath (1Sa 17:1).

With Lachish it was among the last fenced cities to fall to Babylon (Jer 34:7).

📖 Key Scripture

Josh 10:11 — "And it came to pass, as they fled from before Israel, and were in the going down to Bethhoron, that the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them unto Azekah, and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword."

1Sa 17:1 — "Now the Philistines gathered together their armies to battle, and were gathered together at Shochoh, which belongeth to Judah, and pitched between Shochoh and Azekah, in Ephesdammim."

Jer 34:7 — "When the king of Babylon's army fought against Jerusalem, and against all the cities of Judah that were left, against Lachish, and against Azekah: for these defenced cities remained of the cities of Judah."

2Ch 11:9 — "And Adoraim, and Lachish, and Azekah,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

A place-name, not a doctrine in dispute; its lesson spans God’s deliverance and His judgment upon an impenitent people.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the same God who delivered Israel at Azekah by hailstones, and gave the giant into David’s hand near its walls, also gave Azekah up to Babylon when Judah would not repent. The Lord who saves is the Lord who judges; His patience is long, but His justice is sure, and a people who spurn His mercy will at last meet His rod.

Azekah at the field of Ephes-dammim also enshrines the lesson of David and Goliath: the battle is the LORD’s, and He saves not with sword and spear. The youth who came in the name of the LORD of hosts overthrew the champion of the Philistines, that all the earth might know there is a God in Israel. Faith in the living God, not the arm of flesh, is the strength of His people.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The name is read as “tilled” or “dug,” perhaps of a place hedged and worked for defence.

expand to see more

Azekah — Hebrew Azeqah, perhaps “tilled” or “dug over.”

It stood in the Shephelah, the lowland between the hills and the coast.

It guarded a road descending from Judah toward the Philistines.

Rehoboam numbered it among his fortified cities.

It was among the last strongholds of Judah to fall.

Usage

"Like Judah at Azekah, a people may know God’s deliverance and yet, refusing repentance, meet His judgment."

"Azekah recalls that the battle is the LORD’s, who saves not with sword and spear."

"The hailstones unto Azekah witness that the Lord of hosts fights for His people from heaven."
